topics.title: Chapter overview
topics.summary: A TCP connection delivers bytes in order, but it does not deliver the application messages that the programmer imagined when calling send. One write can arrive through several reads, and several writes can be observed together. A receiving program must define message boundaries, validate lengths, and interpret fields independently of its in-memory object layout.

topics.title: 7.1.1 Defining Framing and Size Limits
topics.summary: Framing determines where one message ends and the next begins. Common choices include a fixed size, a delimiter, a length prefix, or an established protocol with its own framing. Each choice needs rules for malformed input and resource limits. A delimiter is simple only if escaping, binary data, and maximum line length are also defined.

blocks.text: The companion uses a four-byte unsigned big-endian payload length followed by at most 4,096 payload bytes. The header is parsed before allocating unbounded storage. A declared length above the limit makes the connection invalid immediately. The decoder rejects extra bytes supplied beyond one complete frame. The server dispatches as soon as one frame is complete and closes after its response; it does not wait for the peer to declare EOF. Consequently, bytes arriving only after dispatch are not evidence that an earlier effect was rolled back. The protocol does not support pipelined requests.

blocks.text: A length prefix is not a trust boundary by itself. An attacker or defective peer can declare a huge length, send a partial header, or close before the payload completes. The decoder must distinguish incomplete input from invalid input, and the connection must impose a waiting deadline. Without both a byte bound and a time bound, a small-looking protocol can still consume resources indefinitely.

The companion maintains a small established maximum and subtracts the current size from that maximum before admitting more bytes.

topics.title: 7.1.2 Keeping Decoding Incremental and Deterministic
topics.summary: An incremental decoder retains state across input chunks. Its behavior should depend on the byte sequence, not on how the operating system happened to partition that sequence into reads. This is a property that can be tested without a network by feeding every split of a known message.

blocks.text: A useful decoder API separates “need more input” from “invalid input.” Throwing on every partial header would make ordinary network fragmentation look like corruption. Treating an invalid length as merely incomplete would let a peer hold resources while waiting for a message the application must never accept.

blocks.text: Golden-byte tests are important. An encoder and decoder that share the same endian bug can agree with each other while disagreeing with every other implementation. Compare at least a few encoded messages with independently specified bytes, and then test round trips and fragmentation. Agreement between two functions written from the same mistaken assumption is not an independent oracle.

topics.title: 7.2.1 Avoiding Raw Object Serialization
topics.summary: A C++ object’s memory representation is not a portable wire format. Padding, alignment, byte order, pointer values, enum representation, and compiler layout choices can differ. Even a trivially copyable type is not automatically a cross-platform protocol record. Copying its bytes may be valid for a narrow in-process operation while remaining unsuitable for persistent or remote interchange.

topics.title: 7.2.2 Using Schema-Based Serialization Deliberately
topics.summary: A schema language can define field numbers, types, messages, and services independently of C++ classes. Protocol Buffers generates language bindings from such definitions. Its binary evolution rules depend on preserving field identities and respecting compatible changes; removed field numbers should not be reused for unrelated meanings. Unknown-field behavior and JSON conversion have their own constraints. (R14)

topics.title: 7.3.1 Distinguishing Additive Fields from Semantic Changes
topics.summary: Adding an optional field can be wire-compatible while changing behavior in a way old peers cannot honor. Suppose a new request includes a “do not execute twice” option but an old worker ignores it. The message may decode successfully, yet the caller’s safety requirement is not met. Compatibility must include meaning, not just parser acceptance.

blocks.text: A second family of tests handles declared length rather than actual length. A prefix announcing 4097 bytes must be rejected under the 4096-byte contract without waiting for or allocating the entire payload. A prefix announcing three bytes followed by only two must remain incomplete and fail when end-of-input is declared. When extra bytes are fed to the decoder, a complete frame followed by another byte violates its one-frame contract and must be rejected. At the server boundary, dispatch can precede a later arrival of unsolicited bytes; closing that connection cannot undo an effect already committed. Decoder validation and transactional rollback are different boundaries.
